finding: Test 9's observable is the one value the named killing mutation cannot move. It asserts that switching to `blocking` without re-recording "leaves every stored round's verdict unchanged", and names the review twin's live re-grade as the mutation that kills it. Measured against the twin: the review side ALSO stamps at record time -- internal/cli/review_record.go:141 writes `Clean: clean` into state.json and its comment at 189-191 says "the stored ReviewRound.Clean stays the frozen record-time value"; internal/cli/review_status.go:60 says of the live recompute "(this response is not persisted)". So under the live-re-grade design the STORED verdict is byte-identical to the stamped design, and a test written to test 9's own words (record, flip the knob, re-read state.json, compare) passes against its killing mutation. The only observable that separates the two designs is the REPORTED verdict.
suggestion: Reword test 9's observable as the reported verdict on both audit outputs, not the stored one: after recording under `all` and setting `blocking` with no re-record, `tp audit <spec> --status` must emit the same `audit_rounds[].clean` per round, the same `consecutive_clean` and the same `converged` as before the switch, and a `--record` of an unchanged results file must emit the same `clean`. State that reading state.json alone does not discriminate, so the next draft does not re-derive it.

finding: Test 9 pins no property of its fixture, so even with the observable corrected the named mutation survives on most fixtures an implementer would build. A live re-grade changes the answer only for a round whose non-PASS rows are ALL non-blocking (warning/info only); on a round with zero non-PASS rows, or on one carrying an `error`, `all` and `blocking` agree and the mutation is invisible. Measured on this repository's corpus, 4 of v0.35.0's 9 audit rounds and 3 of v0.36.0's 13 agree under both policies, so a two-round fixture drawn without the rule has a real chance of proving nothing. Secondly, engine.ReviewRoundClean falls back to the stored flag when the round's findings file is missing (internal/engine/reviewclean.go:57-60), so a fixture that synthesises state.json entries without writing audit-round-N.ndjson also survives the mutation.
suggestion: Require the fixture to be self-guarding, in the same way brief_runs_test.go's `require.NotEmpty` guards its divergent fixture: at least one recorded round must carry non-PASS rows of which none is `error` (so its verdict differs between the two policies) and the test must assert that precondition before the comparison; and every recorded round must have a real audit-round-N.ndjson on disk, recorded through `--record`, not a synthesised state entry.

finding: Test 13 is the only test in the list that names neither an input nor a mutation, against §7's own opening rule that "Each test names the input that makes it fail" -- tests 5/6/7 name a severity, 8 names three fixtures, 9 names the live re-grade, 10 names the re-recording. "Correct over a mixed round" leaves the fixture entirely open, and one omission is load-bearing: §4 restricts by_severity to non-`PASS` rows, and a fixture of only non-PASS rows cannot test that restriction. Measured, an implementation counting every row would bucket PASS rows under the no-severity key, because all 2,913 PASS rows in v0.35.0+v0.36.0 carry `severity: null` -- so the restriction is only observable when the fixture carries PASS rows too. Two engineers write different fixtures and only one of them can fail.
suggestion: Pin test 13's fixture and its killing mutation: a round carrying at least one PASS row (whose severity must NOT appear in by_severity), one `error`, one `warning`, one `info`, one row with a severity outside the enum and one with none; assert the exact map, not just presence. Name the two mutations: counting all rows rather than non-PASS rows, and moving the assignment inside `--merge`'s existing `if !IsCompact()` block (internal/cli/audit_merge.go:90).

finding: §4's keying rule for by_severity is undefined over two of the four row shapes the release must handle, so test 13's "correct" cannot be written deterministically. (a) "one with none under `null`": a JSON object key is a string, so this is `{"null": 1}`, `{"": 1}`, or a key omitted entirely -- three incompatible readings, and the count is decision-relevant because §4 says the breakdown "never hides a row the predicate would block on". (b) "a row with an unrecognised severity is counted under the literal it carries" is undefined when the literal is not a string: nothing rejects `"severity": 3` or `"severity": true` on the audit path (audit_record.go validates `category` only), and Go's `row["severity"].(string)` collapses a number, a bool and an absent key to the same empty string -- so the natural implementation silently merges cases (a) and (b), which is precisely the hiding §4 forbids. Measured: every severity in all 360 recorded non-PASS rows is a string, so the corpus supplies no instance and this will first appear in the field.
suggestion: State the key for each shape as a literal: absent or JSON `null` -> key `"null"`; a non-empty string -> that string verbatim; any other JSON type -> its compact JSON encoding (`"3"`, `"true"`) rather than being folded into the null bucket. Add the non-string row to test 13's fixture and to test 8's fail-closed fixtures, which today enumerate three shapes and imply completeness.

finding: No test guards Non-Goal 2 against the predicate this release adds, and the failure mode is the same "natural thing to copy" that test 9 exists to block. `tp audit --resolve` ships today (internal/cli/audit_resolve.go) and writes a `resolved` object onto a row; the record path deliberately ignores it -- countAuditFindings (audit_record.go:248) counts every non-PASS row regardless. The model an implementer will reach for when writing the audit severity predicate is engine.ReviewRoundClean, whose surviving set is computed by reviewFindingResolvedAway (reviewclean.go:32-43,64-66). Copying that helper along with the severity test ships Non-Goal 2 -- a disposition that stops blocking -- while every test in §7 stays green, because tests 5-8 use rows that carry no `resolved` key at all.
suggestion: Add a test: a round whose only non-PASS row is `error` carrying `resolved: {status: "wontfix", evidence: "..."}` is NOT clean under either value of audit_converge_on, and the round's recorded `findings` count still includes it. Name the killing mutation as folding reviewFindingResolvedAway (or rowDisposed) into the audit clean predicate.

finding: Test 11 has no negative control, so an over-broad fence passes it while breaking every unattended write. It asserts only that the three paths exit 2 for `all` and `blocking` and "0 without it" -- i.e. the 0 case is the fence DISABLED, never the fence enabled on a write that does not touch this field. Under TP_UNATTENDED=1, `tp set --workflow audit_clean_rounds=2` and a `tp import` of a task file whose workflow block omits audit_converge_on must both still exit 0; nothing in §7 says so. This is a live risk rather than a hypothetical: the existing hook, fenceWorkflowWrite (internal/cli/unattended.go:56), takes `requested float64` and is dispatched per field, so a string-valued field cannot use it and an implementer must add a new branch -- the cheapest of which fences the command, not the field.
suggestion: Add to test 11 the enabled-fence zero case on all three paths: under TP_UNATTENDED=1, a `tp set --workflow`, a `tp set --workflow --project` and a `tp import` that do not mention audit_converge_on each exit 0 and write what they were asked to write.

finding: §3's two normative sentences give opposite answers on a third input that `tp import` really produces, and test 11 tests only two. "Every path that WRITES the field" reads as: fence when the incoming document mentions audit_converge_on. "The fence is on the field, not the direction" reads as: fence whenever the effective value moves. They diverge on a REMOVAL. Measured in internal/cli/importcmd.go:154-162, workflow preservation applies only when the imported document carries no top-level `workflow` key; a `{...}` import whose workflow block is present but omits audit_converge_on therefore REPLACES a target's stored `blocking` with nothing, changing the resolved value to the built-in `all` -- a write of the field by the second reading and not by the first. Test 11 pins "for both `all` and `blocking`", so both implementations pass it and they disagree on real input.
suggestion: Decide the removal case in §3 in one sentence -- e.g. "a write that removes the key from a layer that carried it is a write of the field and is refused on the same terms" -- and add it to test 11 as a third input on the tp import path, with the fixture being an existing task file carrying audit_converge_on=blocking and an imported document whose workflow block omits it.

finding: Test 12's natural assertion cannot fail against the defect §3 names, and its two halves are one assertion where §7 elsewhere insists on two. §3 forbids "reusing one written for command fields"; that message is refuseUnattendedCommandField's (internal/cli/unattended.go:44-48), `"%s names a command the driver executes and cannot be set under TP_UNATTENDED, at any layer"` -- which interpolates the field name, so `Contains(out, "audit_converge_on")` passes against the exact reuse the test exists to catch. The cap message at line 33-37 interpolates it too. Separately, "the escalation records --decision audit-converge-on rather than other" spans two independent sinks: the hint tp prints (built from escalationDecision(field), unattended.go:19-27, which returns "other" for anything unnamed) and `tp escalate`'s closed enum (engine.EscalationDecisions, five members today). §7 applies the two-sinks-two-assertions rule explicitly in tests 3 and 11 and not here, so an implementation that adds the enum member but leaves the hint at "other" -- or fixes the hint and leaves the enum, making tp print a command that then exits 2 -- passes a test written to test 12's words.
suggestion: Split test 12 into three assertions with named mutations: (a) the refusal message must NOT contain the command-field wording ("names a command the driver executes") nor the cap wording -- a negative assertion, since every candidate message contains the field name; (b) the printed hint carries `--decision audit-converge-on`, mutation: escalationDecision returning "other"; (c) `tp escalate --decision audit-converge-on --evidence <x>` exits 0 and the written record validates, mutation: leaving engine.escalationDecisions at its five members.

finding: Test 14's title claims a quantifier the test it describes cannot check. "The three reversals and nothing more" is an exhaustiveness claim over every assertion in the suite, while the described procedure checks two named assertions in one guard plus two documentation strings. Nothing in it could fail on a fourth reversal elsewhere, and the procedure a reader would substitute -- run the suite, see it green -- is a tautology: a reversed assertion is one that was rewritten to pass, so a green suite after the change is evidence of nothing about how many were changed. This is the repository's own "never assert a quantifier you did not count" rule applied to a test rather than to prose, and it is the one test whose failure would tell a reader that the release touched more than it claimed.
suggestion: Either drop "and nothing more" and let test 14 assert only what it checks, or bind the quantifier to an artifact that can drift-check itself -- e.g. commit the three reversed assertions as a named list and have the task's acceptance derive the diff of changed assertions from `git diff` against that list, in task acceptance where it is checked by running, per this file's own rewrite banner.

finding: Near-miss, reported as asked. I opened six of this spec's measured claims intending to falsify them and every one is exact against the corpus, so no round should re-open them: §1's "42 non-PASS rows: 3 error, 22 warning, 17 info" for v0.35.0; §2's "2,913 PASS rows carry severity: null" (1758 + 1155, and all 2,913 are JSON null); §2's "67 non-PASS rows across v0.29.0-v0.32.0 carry severities outside the enum, in fifteen round files" (67 rows -- 36 low, 16 high, 15 medium -- in exactly 15 files, all inside that version range); §2.1's four convergence cells at audit_clean_rounds 2 (v0.35.0 blocking round 3 / all round 9; v0.36.0 blocking round 3 / all never, no round reaching zero); test 10's "at 1 the first pair is 2 and 8"; test 6's "158 of the corpus's 360 non-PASS rows" (warning 158, info 109, low 36, error 26, high 16, medium 15 = 360). I also checked two feasibility risks for test 10 and both are clear: no recorded audit row in v0.35.0 or v0.36.0 carries a category outside the five-value enum, so re-recording the committed testdata will not abort in countAuditFindings' category check (audit_record.go:252); and test 8's "a legacy row supplies only the first" is correct -- none of the 67 out-of-enum severities is null or absent.
suggestion: No change. Recorded so a later round does not spend itself re-deriving these; the derivation is a single pass over spec/.tp-review/*/audit-round-*.ndjson.
